title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array
directAnswer: Remove duplicates in place from a sorted array and return the count k of unique values. The naive answer copies uniques into a new array; the canonical answer uses a slow write pointer and a fast read pointer — whenever nums[fast] differs from the last kept value, advance slow and copy. Return slow + 1.

remember.formula:
if n == 0: return 0
slow = 0
for fast in 1..n-1:
    if nums[fast] != nums[slow]:
        slow += 1
        nums[slow] = nums[fast]
return slow + 1
rules: `slow` marks the **last unique** kept; `fast` scans ahead for the next new value.
Compare `nums[fast]` to `nums[slow]` — the array is **sorted**, so duplicates are adjacent.
Only write when you find a **new** value, so you never overwrite an element you still need.
Return the **count** `slow + 1`, not the array — the first `k` slots hold the answer.
Handle the empty array up front: `n == 0` must return `0`.
`slow` is a **length-minus-one** index, so the unique count is always `slow + 1`.
whenToUse: Sorted array where equal elements are guaranteed adjacent
You need the count of distinct elements, leftover tail can be ignored
The 'keep some, drop the rest' family — dedup, remove-element, move-zeroes
antiSignals: Array is unsorted → duplicates aren't adjacent; sort first or use a hash set
You must preserve every duplicate's position → this destroys them
Need the removed elements too → don't overwrite, collect instead
Order doesn't matter and you can allocate → a set is simpler
remember.takeaway: Two pointers moving at different speeds — a slow write head and a fast read head — is the canonical way to compact an array in place. Because the input is sorted, equal values cluster, so a single adjacent comparison decides keep-or-skip. The same slow/fast shape solves Remove Element, Move Zeroes, and Remove Duplicates II.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you exploit the sorted property (duplicates are adjacent) to dedup in O(1) space with two pointers, instead of reaching for a set or a second array.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Returning the array instead of the count k, or using a single index for both reading and writing so you overwrite values before comparing them.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Note that 'sorted' means equal values are adjacent — that's the property that lets one comparison (nums[fast] vs nums[slow]) decide everything. Mention the slow pointer is a length-minus-one index, so return slow + 1.

problemStatement:
Given an integer array `nums` sorted in **non-decreasing order**, remove the duplicates *in place* such that each unique element appears only **once**. The *relative order* of the elements should be kept the same. Then return the number of unique elements in `nums`.

Consider the number of unique elements of `nums` to be `k`. To get accepted, you need to do the following:

- Change the array `nums` such that the first `k` elements of `nums` contain the unique elements in the order they were present initially. The remaining elements of `nums` are not important as well as the size of `nums`.
- Return `k`.
constraints: nums is sorted in non-decreasing order
understanding: Because the array is sorted, every run of equal values is contiguous. We keep the first element of each run and skip the rest, packing the survivors into the front of the array. We return how many survivors there are; whatever sits past index k−1 is ignored by the judge.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the array guaranteed sorted?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, non-decreasing. That's the linchpin — it means duplicates are adjacent, so a single comparison to the previous kept value suffices.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do I return the array or a number?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: A number: k, the count of unique elements. The judge then reads only nums[0..k-1].

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does the order of the unique elements matter?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, original relative order must be preserved. Since the array is sorted, scanning left to right preserves it automatically.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the array be empty?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The constraints say length ≥ 1, but it's good practice to guard n == 0 → return 0 so the code is robust.

examples.explanation: Unique values are 1 and 2. The first two slots hold them; the underscore is don't-care.
Five distinct values; the rest of the array is irrelevant.
A single element is trivially unique.

diagrams.title: Why sorted unlocks two pointers

approaches.name: Copy Uniques to a New Array (Naive)
approaches.whenToMention: A clear baseline to state first — then point out it breaks the in-place / O(1)-space requirement.
hints: Forget in-place for a second: how would you list the distinct values of a sorted array into a fresh list?
Append nums[i] whenever it differs from the previous element (or it's the first element).
That list IS the uniques in order. To satisfy the in-place spec you'd then copy it back into nums and return its length — which is exactly the extra space we want to avoid.
approaches.complexityReasoning: One linear scan to build the list (O(n) time), plus a result list that can hold up to n elements (O(n) space). Copying back is another O(n) pass but doesn't change the asymptotics.
approaches.explanation:
Scan left to right and collect each value that differs from its predecessor into a separate list. Because the array is sorted, that list is precisely the set of unique values in their original order. To honour the in-place contract you'd copy the list back into `nums` and return its size.

**Why this is the natural first attempt.** "Remove duplicates" reads like "build the list of things that aren't duplicates". Allocating a fresh container and appending the survivors is the most direct mental model — no pointer juggling, no overwrite hazards, just a filter. It's correct and easy to reason about.

**Why the comparison is to the previous element.** In a sorted array, a value is a duplicate exactly when it equals the one just before it. So `nums[i]` is new iff `i == 0 || nums[i] != nums[i-1]`. That single test is all the dedup logic you need — the sortedness does the rest.

**Why it falls short of the spec.** The problem explicitly demands an in-place transformation with the answer living in `nums[0..k-1]`. A separate list uses `O(n)` auxiliary memory, which defeats the purpose — and the copy-back is busywork. Interviewers pose this exact problem to see whether you can avoid the extra array.

**Why we still mention it.** It anchors correctness: it's obvious the filtered list is right. From there, the leap is realising the destination buffer can be `nums` *itself*, written by a second pointer that always trails the reader — which is the optimal solution.
approaches.insight: The filter rule 'keep nums[i] when it differs from nums[i-1]' is the entire algorithm in one line. The only thing wrong with the naive version is *where* it writes — a new array. Redirect those writes into the front of nums and the extra space vanishes.

dryRun.intro: Append each value that differs from the previous one into a result list.

java.explanation: A value is new iff it's the first or differs from its predecessor — sortedness makes this sufficient.
Collect the survivor into the auxiliary list — the O(n) space we want to eliminate.
k is the number of uniques collected.

python.explanation: New value test: first element, or different from the previous.
Build the uniques in order — the extra list is the cost.
Copy back into nums so the front holds the answer.

edgeCases.behavior: Only the first 2 is appended; k = 1.

pitfalls: Allocating a list defeats the O(1)-space goal — fine as a baseline, not as the final answer.
Forgetting to copy the list back into nums — the judge inspects nums itself.
Returning the list instead of its length.

approaches.name: Slow/Fast Two Pointers (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Phrase it as 'a slow write pointer trailing a fast read pointer'.
hints: You don't need a second array — you can reuse the front of nums as the output region. What invariant would let you safely overwrite slots you've already passed?
Keep slow = index of the last unique value written, and fast scanning ahead. Everything in nums[0..slow] is the deduped prefix so far.
When nums[fast] differs from nums[slow], it's a new unique: increment slow and copy nums[fast] there. fast always leads slow, so you never overwrite an unread value. Return slow + 1.
approaches.complexityReasoning: fast makes one pass over the array (O(n)); each step does O(1) work. slow only ever advances, and we use a constant number of variables → O(1) extra space.
approaches.explanation:
Maintain two indices. `slow` is the position of the last unique value we've committed to the front of the array; `fast` races ahead looking for the next value that breaks the current run. The region `nums[0..slow]` is always the correctly deduplicated prefix.

**The invariant that makes it safe.** At every moment, `nums[0..slow]` contains the unique values seen so far, in order, and `fast > slow` always. Because the write pointer `slow` never catches up to the read pointer `fast`, any slot we overwrite (`nums[slow+1]`) is one `fast` has already moved past — its original content is no longer needed. This is the same write-head-trails-read-head guarantee that makes in-place array compaction possible without a buffer.

**Why one comparison is enough.** The array is sorted, so all copies of a value form a contiguous block. The first element of each block is the one we keep; the rest equal it. So `nums[fast]` is a *new* value precisely when `nums[fast] != nums[slow]` — we compare against the last kept value, not a whole set. When they're equal, `fast` is still inside the current run and we simply skip; when they differ, `fast` has entered a new run, so we advance `slow` and copy. Sortedness collapses 'have I seen this before?' from a set membership query into a single adjacent comparison.

**Why we write at `slow + 1`, not `slow`.** `slow` already holds a committed unique value we must not clobber. The next unique belongs in the slot immediately after it. So on a new value we first do `slow++` to open the next slot, then `nums[slow] = nums[fast]`. Doing it in the other order would overwrite the value we just kept.

**Why the answer is `slow + 1`.** `slow` is the *index* of the last unique, and indices are zero-based, so the *count* of uniques is `slow + 1`. The leftover tail past index `slow` still holds stale values, but the problem says those slots are don't-care, so we leave them. Guard the empty array (`n == 0 → 0`) since `slow` starting at `0` assumes at least one element exists.
approaches.insight: Two pointers at different speeds turn a 'filter into a new array' problem into an in-place overwrite. The crucial realisation is that the survivors are always fewer than the elements scanned, so a trailing write pointer can never overtake the reader — the front of the array doubles as your output buffer for free.

dryRun.intro: slow=0 (first element is always unique). fast scans from 1. Copy on a new value.

java.explanation: The first element is always unique, so slow starts at index 0 holding it.
Compare to the LAST kept value; sortedness means a difference signals a brand-new value.
Open the next slot AFTER the last unique — order matters so we don't clobber it.
Copy the new unique forward; fast > slow guarantees this slot is free to overwrite.
slow is a zero-based index, so the unique count is slow + 1.

python.explanation: Index of the last committed unique; element 0 is unique by definition.
One adjacent comparison decides keep-or-skip because equal values are contiguous.
Advance the write head before writing so the previous unique survives.
Place the new unique into the front region.

diagrams.title: Write head never overtakes read head
diagrams.caption: fast > slow always, so nums[slow+1] is always a slot fast already left behind.

edgeCases.behavior: The fast loop never runs; return slow + 1 = 1.
Every comparison is equal, slow stays 0, return 1.
Every value is new, slow ends at 2, return 3; array is unchanged.

pitfalls: Writing nums[slow] = nums[fast] before incrementing slow — overwrites the last kept unique.
Comparing nums[fast] to nums[fast-1] works too, but comparing to nums[slow] is the canonical, copy-safe form.
Returning slow instead of slow + 1 — off by one.
Forgetting the empty-array guard when starting slow at 0.

commonMistakes: Returning the array (or slow) instead of the count slow + 1.
Using a single index for both reading and writing, overwriting unread values.
Using a hash set — correct but wastes the sorted property and O(n) space.
Incrementing slow after the copy instead of before, clobbering the last unique.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Off-by-one on the return value
commonMistakesDetailed.why: slow is the zero-based INDEX of the last unique, not the count. The number of uniques is slow + 1; returning slow undercounts by one.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Writing before advancing the write head
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Doing nums[slow] = nums[fast] and then slow++ overwrites the unique value currently at slow, corrupting the prefix.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Reaching for a hash set on a sorted array
commonMistakesDetailed.why: A set ignores the sorted structure and spends O(n) extra space. The whole point is that sortedness makes one adjacent comparison enough for O(1) space.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
seen = set()
k = 0
for x in nums:
    if x not in seen:
        seen.add(x)
        nums[k] = x
        k += 1
return k

followupVariations.hint: Allow each value at most twice — compare nums[fast] to nums[slow-1] instead of nums[slow].

followupVariations.hint: Same slow/fast compaction, but the keep condition is nums[fast] != val.

followupVariations.title: Move Zeroes
followupVariations.hint: Keep non-zeros with a write pointer, then fill the tail with zeros.

followupVariations.hint: Same idea on a linked list — skip nodes equal to the current head.

patternNote: Canonical slow/fast two-pointer compaction. Recognise it whenever you must keep some elements and drop others in place, in order, with O(1) space. The sorted input lets a single adjacent comparison decide each element. Same shape as Remove Element, Move Zeroes, and Remove Duplicates II.
